rv.q: The famous helicopter scene may not be as jaw-dropping as it was inthe original Eightiesstaging, but after a 15-year absence Miss Saigon makes astirring return to the West End. It's less operatic than before and has a grittier feel. Yet it remains a huge spectacle, and the music (by Claude-Michel SchonbergandAlainBoublil) surges and soars.
For all its many merits, however, I find it easier to admire Miss Saigon than to love it.
In this new production by Laurence Connor, it survives very well as a piece of musical storytelling and as a public spectacle.
I'll forgive Miss Saigon a lot for the vivid way it depicts the fallout from an impossible love.
Sir Cameron Mackintosh's revival of the 1980s musical Miss Saigon is staged with such insistent extravagance that it bludgeons its way to success. Great art? Nope. But big theatre.
Laurence Connor's revival is as powerfully built as its firm-jawed American Marine hero, but it could be more honed.
So Mackintosh's monster musical still impresses, but one wonders if even the Mack really knows how to control a show this big anymore.
No wonder the clapping did not come from me.
Such a wave of raw emotion ought to be suffocating but the sincerity of the story and production ensure you’ll be overwhelmed by Miss Saigon in the best way possible.
Ms. Noblezada proves a sensation in the part.

While Laurence Connor ‘s competent revival presses most of the right buttons in this melodramatic re-write of Madame Butterfly during and after the evacuation from Saigon in 1975, it’s neither as good as, nor better than, Nicholas Hytner ‘s 1989 operatic original.
This is a visually stunning, exciting production that will not disappoint and is likely to continue to break hearts for many years to come.
This is a sung-through recitative packed with ballads more powerful than memorable.

Miss Saigon managed, what all theatre should do, to create a magical world where despite the unrealistic song and dance, was easily a, what one would assume, realistic representation of this historical period – but theatrically sound and relatable for audiences all the same.
The lush score, overladen with power ballads, grows wearing, and, for all its proficiency, the production remains stubbornly unmoving.
Miss Saigon is a stunning musical and will entertain audiences for many years to come but this revival doesn’t quite live up to die-hard fan’s expectations.

cn.t: This lavish revival delivers spectacular staging and Schönberg's soaring score, but critics find it more blockbuster spectacle than artistic depth, with mixed views on whether it matches the original's impact.
